title: Hot spots: six conflicts, and the one question that sorts them
hook:
This week Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed that a supertanker had struck a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. Nobody has confirmed it. It barely matters. In recent weeks more tankers were attacked around the strait than in any week since the war began, and every shipping desk from Singapore to Rotterdam was pricing the risk that the claim was true. Brent crude was back near its spring high. In India, that one sentence from the Gulf runs straight into the petrol pump, the LPG cylinder, the rupee and the RBI's next decision.

Meanwhile, Chinese warships were holding live-fire drills around Taiwan, North Korea was firing missiles, Russia and Ukraine were trading strikes under an energy ceasefire neither side had confirmed, and Chinese and Philippine boats were jostling over reefs in the South China Sea. Six live conflicts, all loud.

But they are not equally important for an Indian portfolio. One is a hot war already moving oil every day. The rest are pressure points that matter only if they escalate into the channels India cares about. This chapter, the one part of the framework refreshed every week, sorts them with a single question: does it touch oil, or chips?
short: Six conflicts matter for Indian markets this autumn, but only the Iran war is moving prices every day, through oil, freight and the rupee.
Read the heat matrix by column: a conflict that lights up oil or chips matters more for India than one that only fills headlines.

The escalation ladders show where each conflict stands and what the next step up would be; each rung up in the Iran war has meant a higher war premium in oil, and a ceasefire takes it out just as fast.
Taiwan and Korea are the tail risks that would hurt most, through the chips inside every phone, car and AI server; Russia–Ukraine reaches India through sanctions on crude.
Size hedges to oil, not to headlines.

sections.heading: How to read the heat matrix: by column, not by row
sections.html:
Start with the big picture. Every conflict on earth can reach an Indian portfolio, but only through a few pipes: the price of oil and gas, the cost of shipping, the supply of chips and components, the mood of global investors, sanctions and trade rules, and direct effects on India itself, such as remittances, defence orders or Indian firms caught up in sanctions.

[[fig:1]]

The matrix puts the conflicts in rows and those pipes in columns. A dark cell marked high means the conflict is already moving that channel, or would move it sharply on escalation. Medium and low are what they sound like, and a blank cell means no meaningful link. The tag under each conflict's name is the trend over the past month: escalating, elevated or calm.

Here's the trick: read it by column, not by row. The rows tell you which conflict is loudest. The columns tell you what matters for India. Run your eye down the oil column and there is one dark cell: the Iran war. Run it down the chips column and there is another: Taiwan. The global risk appetite column is how distant wars reach India even when they touch nothing Indian, because when global investors get scared they sell emerging markets, and Indian shares are easy to sell.

Notice also the last column. Only two rows score there: the Iran war, which reaches Indian kitchens, current account and remittances directly, and India's own borders, which reach defence spending. That tells you something the news channels won't: the Line of Control, for all its drama, currently matters less to Indian stocks than a strait off the coast of Oman. This is our assessment, refreshed weekly from the news desk and a web check, so treat it as a judgement, not a measurement.

sections.heading: Why one narrow strait matters more than every other hot spot
sections.html:
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow channel between Iran and Oman. About a fifth of the world's oil passes through it, along with much of the liquefied natural gas from Qatar, India's largest LNG supplier. There is no real way around it for most Gulf producers. Close Hormuz and you do not just raise the price of oil, you remove barrels from the market altogether.

India is unusually exposed. It imports most of the crude it uses, and much of it comes from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait, all of which ship through the strait. Most of the LPG in Indian kitchens comes from the Gulf too. Here is how a Hormuz shock travels through the economy, step by step.

  • The import bill. Pricier oil means India spends more dollars on the same barrels, which widens the current account deficit, the gap between what India earns from the world and what it pays.
  • The rupee. More dollars going out weakens the rupee, which makes the oil dearer still in rupee terms.
  • Inflation and rates. Fuel, freight and fertiliser costs feed into prices, and the RBI has to respond. The October 2026 rate hike was exactly this chain at work.
  • The budget. The government either cuts fuel taxes or lets state-run oil companies absorb losses; both cost money.
  • Remittances. Millions of Indians work in the Gulf. A war there threatens the money they send home.

The sectors that feel it first are easy to list once you see the chain. Airlines, because jet fuel is their biggest single cost. Oil marketing companies, because pump prices are sticky and they often eat the difference. Paint makers, because many of their raw materials are derived from crude. Consumer goods firms, through packaging and freight. Logistics companies, through diesel. And a handful of Indian firms have been named in US sanctions on Iranian trade, a reminder that the direct channel can bite too.

sections.heading: The Iran war, rung by rung
sections.html:
An escalation ladder is a simple way to track a conflict. Each rung is a step more serious than the one below, from talks failing at the bottom to the worst plausible outcome at the top. The marker shows where we are; the rung above it is what to watch for.

[[fig:3]]

Climb it with us. At the end of February, after talks failed, the United States and Israel began striking Iran, and Iran retaliated across the region. Then it played its strongest card: it attacked shipping and closed Hormuz. Brent jumped by half in three weeks. In late March President Donald Trump gave Tehran an ultimatum to reopen the strait or see its energy facilities hit, then postponed it. An American air campaign and a naval blockade followed. In April a ceasefire brokered by Pakistan paused the fighting, with talks in Islamabad, and later a memorandum of understanding; oil fell back towards its prewar level. In July the truce collapsed as ships were attacked again. Escorted convoys partly restored the flow, and by late September crude exports through the strait were back near prewar levels.

Then October. Strikes on more than a dozen ships in a single week, the most since the war began, and mines in the water. That is where the marker sits now. The rung above is the tail risk: attacks on the Gulf states' own export terminals, or a long, total closure.

What the ladder teaches is how oil prices the war. Part of the price of a barrel is a war premium, an insurance payment against barrels that might disappear. It rises with every rung and drains just as fast when a ceasefire looks real.

[[fig:2]]

The Brent chart shows exactly that. Look for the double hump: a surge when the war began and the strait closed, a slide back during the ceasefire, and a second climb as the truce collapsed and the tanker war took hold. The markers tie each turn to an event. The Nifty followed the same script, falling when the war began and jumping on the day of the ceasefire.

sections.heading: Russia–Ukraine: the war India trades through
sections.html:
Russia's war in Ukraine reaches India through a different pipe: sanctions. After the 2022 invasion, Western buyers shunned Russian crude and it sold at a discount. Indian refiners, state-owned and private, bought it in huge quantities, and Russia became one of India's biggest oil suppliers almost overnight. It was a windfall for refiners and a cushion for India's import bill.

The catch is that cheap barrels come with legal risk. American sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil, Russia's two biggest oil companies, took effect in late 2025. Nayara Energy, the Gujarat refiner part-owned by Rosneft, has had to rely on Russian oil because many suppliers avoid it. Indian banks that handle payments for these cargoes must watch every transaction for exposure to secondary sanctions, the rules that punish third parties for dealing with sanctioned firms.

This autumn the picture is unusually mixed. The United States announced an energy ceasefire in October, a pause on strikes against power and oil infrastructure, but neither Moscow nor Kyiv has confirmed it and strikes continue. Washington has eased sanctions on Russian diesel, while the European Union approved its largest sanctions package since 2022. Three-way talks have been proposed for late October.

Look back at the matrix: the sanctions column is dark for this row, oil medium, global risk appetite low. Beyond crude, the war touches India through fertiliser and edible-oil prices, since Russia and Ukraine are big exporters of both, and through spare parts for Russian-made weapons in India's armed forces. The sectors most exposed are refiners, banks and chemical makers. The signposts: whether the energy ceasefire is confirmed, what comes out of the talks, and any change in US sanctions on Russian oil.

sections.heading: Taiwan: the tail risk with a chip inside
sections.html:
If Hormuz is the chokepoint for energy, Taiwan is the chokepoint for computing. Almost all of the world's most advanced chips are made on one island, mostly by TSMC. Every smartphone assembled in India, every modern car, every AI server depends on them. A serious crisis would not show up in oil at all, which is why the matrix leaves those cells blank, but it would light up chips and global risk appetite at once.

[[fig:4]]

The Taiwan ladder starts with grey-zone pressure: Chinese aircraft crossing the median line of the strait, coast-guard incidents, actions designed to stay below the threshold of war. The second rung is large live-fire drills and new legal measures, and that is where we are. China began drills across several seas in mid-October, and a revised defence-mobilisation law took effect at the start of the month.

The rung to watch is the third: a quarantine. Unlike a blockade, which is an act of war, a quarantine would be dressed up as law enforcement, with Chinese coast guard ships stopping and inspecting vessels bound for Taiwan. It sounds softer, and that is the point: it is harder for others to respond to. But it would hand Beijing control over what goes in and out of the island. Above that sit a full blockade and armed conflict, a global technology supply shock.

For now, markets are calm. A US official recently argued that investors overprice the risk of conflict. When Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei in August 2022 and China fired missiles around the island, the Nifty barely registered it. India could even gain from the China-plus-one shift. But this is the tail that would hurt most: consumer electronics, autos and IT services would all feel it. Watch for any inspection of shipping, missile deployments near Taiwan, and TSMC's guidance.

sections.heading: The South China Sea and Korea: loud, but not yet expensive
sections.html:
Two more hot spots generate headlines every month without yet costing Indian investors anything.

In the South China Sea, the flashpoint is a reef called Second Thomas Shoal. In 1999 the Philippines deliberately ran an old warship aground there and has kept a handful of marines living on its rusting hull ever since. China's coast guard regularly blocks the boats that resupply them. In July there was a violent boarding, and in early October Philippine vessels were harassed near Thitu island. Why should India care? Partly because the shipping lanes to East Asia carry Indian exports, and partly because the Philippines has a defence treaty with the United States dating from 1951. An incident that triggered it would turn a local quarrel into a US–China confrontation. The signposts: any invocation of that treaty, and the slow ASEAN talks on a code of conduct.

On the Korean peninsula, North Korea fired missiles in October for the fourth time in a month, well over a dozen rounds this year, and a mine exploded on the border in September. There is talk of a summit between Kim Jong Un and Donald Trump. Missile tests have never moved Indian markets. But look at what sits just south of the border: Korea makes most of the world's high-bandwidth memory, the chips that feed AI processors. A real crisis on the peninsula would hit the AI chip chain and Asian risk appetite in one blow.

Loud is not the same as expensive. The market pays for conflicts that reach a channel.

sections.heading: India's own borders, and how to use the cards
sections.html:
The last row of the matrix is India's own borders. They are calm: there has been no escalation with Pakistan or China since the conflict and ceasefire of May 2025. As the previous chapter showed, even when they flare, border events have tended to cost the market a day or two, unless they reach oil, airspace or foreign flows. Their main market channel is defence spending and orders.

Below is one card for each of the six conflicts. Each card has the same five parts, and together they are a weekly routine.

[[fig:5]]
  • Status tells you what happened most recently.
  • Channel into India names the pipe, matching the matrix.
  • Most exposed lists the sector groups that would move first.
  • Signposts are the events that would push the conflict up or down its ladder. This is the part to actually watch.
  • Market memory tells you what similar episodes did to the Nifty, and is honest when we have no evidence either way.

Use the signposts as a checklist. If a ceasefire in the Gulf holds and convoys keep oil moving, the war premium drains. If Gulf export terminals are hit, the next leg up in oil arrives. Everything else is noise until it reaches a channel.

history_title: wars, oil and what markets learned

history.title: The embargo that rewrote the price of energy
history.story:
In October 1973, on the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. When the United States rushed arms to Israel, Arab oil producers, with Saudi Arabia's King Faisal and his oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani at the centre, cut output and embargoed America. Within months the price of oil had roughly quadrupled. Americans queued for hours at petrol stations; parts of Europe banned Sunday driving.

India had no queues for cars, but it felt every barrel. Its oil import bill more than tripled in a year, and prices of grain, edible oil and kerosene soared. In 1974 George Fernandes led a nationwide railway strike over pay eroded by inflation, which the government crushed. That summer Indira Gandhi froze wage increases and curbed company dividends to break the inflation.
history.lesson: Oil wars reprice energy for years, not days, and in India they end up as an inflation and political story.

history.title: The airlift, and the night oil collapsed
history.story:
In August 1990 Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, and the price of oil roughly doubled. Over a hundred thousand Indians were stranded in Kuwait. Air India, Indian Airlines and the Air Force flew them home in an airlift that went into the record books as one of the largest civilian evacuations by air. Their remittances stopped, the oil bill swelled, and India slid towards the balance of payments crisis of 1991.

Then, on a January night in 1991, the US-led air war began. Traders had feared a long, bloody conflict. Instead the first strikes looked overwhelmingly successful, and oil fell by about a third in a single day, the largest one-day drop on record at the time.
history.lesson: Markets bottom when the outcome of a war becomes clear, often before the fighting ends.

history.title: The war rally
history.story:
Through the winter of 2002 and 2003 markets sagged as President George W. Bush built the case for invading Iraq. Nobody knew how long a war would last, what it would do to oil, or whether Saddam would set the oilfields ablaze as he had in Kuwait. When the invasion began in March 2003, stocks rallied. The uncertainty was over.

India's market was about to begin one of its greatest bull runs. The Sensex, which had been stuck for years, started a climb in 2003 that ran until the global crisis of 2008.
history.lesson: The uncertainty before a war often costs markets more than the war itself.

history.title: Crimea, and the shock that stayed at home
history.story:
In March 2014 Vladimir Putin annexed Crimea. The West imposed sanctions, and commentators warned of a new Cold War. Outside Russia, markets barely flinched. The real damage came later and inside Russia: when oil prices crashed late that year, the rouble collapsed and the central bank raised rates dramatically in an emergency move announced in the middle of the night.

For India, 2014 was a year of falling oil and a new government, and the market boomed.
history.lesson: Sanctions shocks are slow and regional at first; they matter globally only when they reach energy.

history.title: Abqaiq: half of Saudi output gone in a morning
history.story:
Early one September morning in 2019, drones and missiles struck Saudi Aramco's giant processing plant at Abqaiq, knocking out more than half of Saudi Arabia's oil output in one blow. When markets opened, Brent posted its biggest one-day jump in decades. It looked like the nightmare scenario.

It wasn't. Aramco restored output within weeks, and prices gave back the spike. In India, the news was quickly drowned out by something bigger: days later, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman slashed corporate tax rates and the Sensex had its best day in a decade.
history.lesson: Oil prices the duration of a disruption, not its drama: damage that can be repaired fast fades fast.

history.title: When a war in Europe reached Indian kitchens
history.story:
In February 2022 Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. The Nifty fell hard that day and kept falling for more than a week. Brent soon hit its highest price since 2008. Sunflower oil, much of which India bought from Ukraine and Russia, became scarce and pushed up the price of every cooking oil. Fertiliser costs spiked. In May the RBI raised rates at a surprise unscheduled meeting, and India banned wheat exports.

India also found an opportunity in the chaos: discounted Russian crude, which its refiners bought by the shipload.
history.lesson: A war that hits energy and food goes global, however far away it starts.

today:
Only one conflict is moving Indian markets right now. Brent is at [[val:brent]] a barrel, up [[val:brent_3m]] over the past three months as the tanker war intensified. The rupee is at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar, not far from its weakest reading of [[val:usdinr_record]], and foreign investors have sold [[val:fii20]] of Indian shares over the last twenty sessions. Strikingly, the India VIX is only [[val:vix]]: the market is pricing the oil shock through the rupee and inflation rather than through panic.

The most important things this week: tanker attacks and mines in Hormuz, with Brent back near its spring high; the unconfirmed Russia–Ukraine energy ceasefire and the talks planned for late October; and China's drills around Taiwan. Watch for a ceasefire in the Gulf that actually holds, whether escorted convoys keep oil flowing, and any strike on Gulf export terminals. This chapter is refreshed weekly, and the same day if the news desk flags a major escalation.
sowhat:
Only the Iran war is moving Indian markets today. Position for the channel, not the noise.

  • Be careful with the sectors on the oil chain: airlines, oil marketing companies, paints, consumer goods with heavy packaging and freight costs, and logistics. They suffer most with each rung up the Iran ladder.
  • Prefer businesses with pricing power or that earn in dollars while the war premium is high; a weak rupee cushions exporters.
  • Size hedges to oil, not to headlines. A loud missile test or a border skirmish rarely justifies a hedge; a rung up in the Gulf does.
  • Keep an eye on the tail risks: Taiwan and Korea would hit electronics, autos and IT through chips. Russia–Ukraine matters for refiners and banks through sanctions.

What would flip it: a Gulf ceasefire that holds, with convoys restoring flows, would drain the war premium quickly, and the oil-chain sectors would have the most to gain. A strike on Gulf export terminals, the top rung, would do the opposite.
